stock-split.summary: Enter a split as new shares for old shares: a 3-for-2 split multiplies quantity by 1.5 and divides proportional per-share amounts by 1.5. A reverse split uses the same convention. This lets you reconcile share count, reference holding value and average acquisition cost without treating a corporate action alone as an investment gain.
stock-split.scope: Manual proportional changes to an intact position. Theoretical fractional shares are retained. No cash-in-lieu, broker rounding, market quotation, lot-level tax reporting, sale or corporate-action eligibility is inferred.

examples.title: A 3-for-2 split turns 120 shares into 180 theoretical shares
examples.inputs: 120 shares before the split; $45 reference market price; $30 average acquisition cost per share; 3 new shares for every 2 old shares.
steps: The new-for-old factor is 3 / 2 = 1.5. Multiply share quantity by that factor.
Divide the reference price by 1.5 to get $30 and average acquisition cost by 1.5 to get $20 per share.
Check the totals: 180 × $30 remains $5,400 of reference value; 180 × $20 remains $3,600 of acquisition cost.
examples.answer: The theoretical holding is 180 shares. The proportional split alone creates no gain in total reference value.

examples.title: A 3-for-2 split followed by a 1-for-5 reverse split leaves 36 shares
examples.inputs: Start with the same 120 shares, $45 reference price and $30 average cost; apply 3-for-2, then 1-for-5 in order.
steps: After the first split, there are 180 theoretical shares. The reverse split then multiplies that quantity by 1 / 5.
The combined factor is (3 / 2) × (1 / 5) = 0.3. Divide the original reference price and per-share cost by 0.3.
The resulting reference price is $150 and average cost $100 per share. Total reference value and acquisition cost stay unchanged.
examples.answer: The intact position has 36 theoretical shares, $5,400 total reference value and $3,600 total acquisition cost.

examples.title: A 1-for-10 reverse split can leave a fractional entitlement
examples.inputs: 103 old shares; $8 reference price; $12 average acquisition cost per old share; 1 new share for every 10 old shares.
steps: Multiply 103 shares by 1 / 10. The theoretical quantity retains the fractional 0.3 share.
Divide the $8 reference price and $12 average cost by 0.1 to get $80 and $120 per new share.
Check the preserved totals: 10.3 × $80 = $824 reference value and 10.3 × $120 = $1,236 acquisition cost. Issuer and broker settlement terms determine actual fractional-share treatment.
examples.answer: The theoretical result is 10.3 new shares. The calculator does not round this to 10 shares or invent a cash-in-lieu payment.

questions.question: Does a 2-for-1 split double my investment value?
questions.answer: It doubles theoretical shares and halves the proportional reference price. That action alone leaves reference value unchanged; market trading can still change prices.

questions.question: How do I enter a 1-for-10 reverse split?
questions.answer: Enter 1 new share and 10 old shares. The factor is 0.1, so 103 old shares give 10.3 theoretical new shares.

questions.question: Does the calculator round fractional shares?
questions.answer: No. It retains theoretical fractions. An issuer or broker’s cash-in-lieu and rounding terms must be handled separately.

questions.question: Is adjusted average acquisition cost a completed tax record?
questions.answer: No. It is an allocation for an intact position. Tax lots, settlements, fees and other corporate actions can require additional records.

customer-acquisition-cost.summary: Customer acquisition cost is the included acquisition spending divided by unique new customers in the same scope. In the itemized example, $25,000 of nonoverlapping costs for 100 new customers gives $250 CAC. Define the customer, time window and included costs before comparing campaigns or channels; a smaller ratio alone does not establish profitability.
customer-acquisition-cost.scope: Manual costs and unique-new-customer counts for a user-defined matching scope. No CRM connection, automatic attribution, customer lifetime value, universal good-CAC threshold or budget recommendation.

examples.title: Reconcile $25,000 of acquisition costs for 100 new customers
examples.inputs: One selected acquisition cohort and reporting window: 100 unique new customers; $12,000 advertising; $8,000 allocated acquisition personnel; $5,000 other acquisition costs; no separate agency or software costs.
steps: Reconcile nonoverlapping costs: $12,000 + $8,000 + $5,000 = $25,000. The personnel and other amounts must not already be included in advertising.
Divide the selected total by 100 unique new customers. Count each newly acquired customer once, even if that customer places multiple orders.
Record whether the window describes a campaign, channel or company-wide cohort so a later comparison uses the same scope.
examples.answer: CAC is $250 per new customer for this defined cost scope. That amount alone does not establish profit or an acceptable advertising budget.

expected.label: Acquisition cost per unique new customer

examples.title: An already reconciled $6,000 total for 40 new customers gives $150 CAC
examples.inputs: A separate selected acquisition cohort: $6,000 known total acquisition cost; 40 unique new customers in the matching scope.
steps: Enter the reconciled cost once rather than entering both the total and its components.
Divide $6,000 by 40. Before comparing it with the $250 example, check customer definitions, included costs, attribution and sales-cycle timing.
examples.answer: CAC is $150 per new customer. The smaller ratio does not by itself prove that this separate cohort is more profitable.

expected.label: Acquisition cost per unique new customer

examples.title: Advertising-only cost is a narrower $120 per customer measure
examples.inputs: Same illustrative 100-new-customer cohort; include $12,000 advertising only; set personnel, agency, software and other costs to zero.
steps: Divide the $12,000 selected advertising cost by the same 100 unique new customers.
Compare with the $250 full-scope illustration: the $130 gap per customer comes from omitting $13,000 of personnel and other costs. The customer count did not change.
Label this as advertising-only cost per new customer. Mixing it with an all-in CAC can make acquisition look cheaper without any operating improvement.
examples.answer: Advertising-only cost is $120 per new customer; the broader example remains $250. State the cost definition beside either figure.

expected.label: Acquisition cost per unique new customer

questions.question: Can I use orders instead of customers?
questions.answer: Only if you intend to calculate cost per order and label it that way. CAC here requires unique new customers in the selected scope.

questions.question: What if no new customers were acquired?
questions.answer: CAC is undefined because its denominator is zero. The calculator identifies that state instead of reporting a real zero cost.

questions.question: Is advertising spend the entire cost of acquisition?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Personnel, agency, software and other allocated acquisition costs can matter. Define and disclose the scope consistently.

questions.question: Does a low CAC prove the business is profitable?
questions.answer: No. Customer revenue, product costs, retention, overhead and future behavior remain separate. The calculator does not apply a universal healthy-CAC threshold.

dividend-discount-model.summary: A dividend discount model values assumed future equity distributions at an entered required return. Stable-growth value uses the next annual dividend divided by required return minus perpetual growth. A two-stage model discounts early dividends separately from a later stable-growth terminal value.
dividend-discount-model.scope: Manual annual end-period dividend assumptions and one annual required equity return. Stable-stage return must exceed growth. No dividend lookup, trading recommendation, automatic growth forecast or tax calculation.

examples.title: Grow the latest $2 dividend before applying Gordon growth
examples.inputs: Latest annual dividend D0 $2 per share; perpetual growth 4%; required annual return 10%.
steps: Calculate the next annual dividend: D1 = $2 × 1.04 = $2.08.
Divide D1 by the rate spread: $2.08 / (0.10 − 0.04). Using D0 directly would miss one growth step.
The perpetual-growth assumption requires the required return to exceed growth. Small changes in that spread can greatly change value.
examples.answer: The assumed dividend stream has a modeled value of about $34.67 per share; this is not a market quote or guaranteed return.

examples.title: Discount two early-growth dividends and a later stable-growth value
examples.inputs: Latest annual dividend $2; 10% growth for two years; 3% perpetual growth afterward; 8% required return.
steps: The first two annual dividends are $2.20 and $2.42. The next dividend for the stable stage is $2.42 × 1.03 = $2.4926.
The terminal price at the end of year two is $2.4926 / (0.08 − 0.03) = $49.852.
Discount year-one dividend once, and both the year-two dividend and terminal price twice. Keep the terminal value at the correct date.
examples.answer: The combined modeled present value is about $46.85 per share under these stated dividend and return assumptions.

questions.question: Do I grow a dividend already entered as D1?
questions.answer: No. D1 is already the next annual dividend. Only a latest dividend entered as D0 is grown once in stable mode.

questions.question: Can perpetual growth equal required return?
questions.answer: Not in this convergent Gordon worksheet. It requires return greater than growth and rejects a zero or negative spread.

questions.question: Does two-stage mode discount the terminal price by N or N+1 years?
questions.answer: By N years. The terminal price at N uses the next dividend D(N+1), then is discounted from time N to time zero.

questions.question: Is the result a predicted trading price?
questions.answer: No. It is an assumption-based dividend valuation. The worksheet does not validate growth, fetch prices or recommend a trade.

earnings-per-share.summary: Basic earnings per share divides period earnings available to common shareholders by weighted average common shares for the same period. Preferred earnings adjustments and the share denominator need a consistent accounting scope. Diluted EPS adds distinct numerator, denominator and anti-dilution considerations.
earnings-per-share.scope: A simplified basic-EPS worksheet using an already-checked preferred earnings adjustment and a supplied average or complete share/day schedule. No automatic diluted EPS, corporate-action restatement or complete reporting compliance.

examples.title: Allocate $900,000 of common earnings over 300,000 average shares
examples.inputs: $1,000,000 period net income; $100,000 entered preferred earnings adjustment; 300,000 weighted average common shares.
steps: Subtract the applicable preferred earnings adjustment: $1,000,000 − $100,000 = $900,000.
Divide common earnings by weighted average common shares for that same period. The adjustment must match the accounting treatment being analyzed.
examples.answer: Basic EPS is $3 per common share. It does not include option, convertible-security or other diluted-EPS adjustments.

examples.title: Weight a share issuance across a 365-day reporting period
examples.inputs: Same $900,000 common earnings; 100,000 common shares for 90 days and 200,000 for the remaining 275 days.
steps: Confirm that 90 + 275 covers all 365 reporting days without overlap.
Divide common earnings by the unrounded weighted average. The 200,000 ending balance is not the average for the full period.
examples.answer: Basic EPS is $5.1328125, displayed to the calculator’s precision. This is a basic-share illustration, not diluted EPS.

questions.question: Can I subtract ordinary common dividends from net income here?
questions.answer: No. The adjustment field is for an already-checked preferred earnings adjustment, not ordinary common-share dividends.

questions.question: Can I enter shares issued instead of shares outstanding in each schedule row?
questions.answer: No. Enter the common shares outstanding for that segment and its day count. Segment days must cover the full reporting period.

questions.question: Can basic EPS be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. A loss attributable to common shareholders divided by positive weighted shares gives negative basic EPS.

questions.question: Does this automatically calculate diluted EPS?
questions.answer: No. Diluted numerator, denominator and anti-dilution rules require separate analysis. This page provides a simplified basic-EPS worksheet.

sharpe-ratio.summary: Sharpe ratio compares arithmetic mean excess return with the standard deviation of those excess returns. The return period and benchmark convention are part of the measure. This worksheet accepts matching-period statistics or a simple return series with a constant same-period risk-free return.
sharpe-ratio.scope: Manual equally spaced simple returns or matched statistics. Series mode uses sample standard deviation (n−1), a fixed same-period risk-free return and an explicit annualization count. No market-price feed, portfolio optimization or performance guarantee.

examples.title: An 8-percentage-point annual excess return over 16% volatility
examples.inputs: Annual arithmetic mean return 12%; annual risk-free return 4%; annual excess-return standard deviation 16%; one observation period per year.
steps: Subtract the matching-period risk-free return: 12% − 4% = 8 percentage points.
Divide 8 by 16. Because the statistics are already annual and the scaling factor is one, no monthly-to-annual conversion is applied.
examples.answer: The Sharpe ratio is 0.5, a dimensionless ratio rather than a 0.5% return or a guarantee of future performance.

expected.label: Sharpe ratio for one observation period

examples.title: Calculate sample volatility from four monthly returns
examples.inputs: Monthly simple returns −2%, 1%, 3% and 0%; constant monthly risk-free return 0%; 12 observations per year for optional scaling.
steps: Arithmetic mean monthly excess return is 0.5%. Use the sample standard deviation, with three degrees of freedom, for these four observations.
Divide the mean by sample volatility to obtain the one-month observation-period ratio.
The optional annualized illustration multiplies that ratio by √12. Correlation and the short sample can make this scaling a poor forecast.
examples.answer: The monthly-period Sharpe ratio is about 0.240192; the assumption-annualized illustration is about 0.832050.

expected.label: Sharpe ratio for one observation period

questions.question: Are Sharpe measure and Sharpe ratio different calculators?
questions.answer: They refer to the same measure on this page. The inputs still need matching periods and a stated benchmark convention.

questions.question: Can I use CAGR as the mean return input?
questions.answer: Not as an automatic substitute. Sharpe uses arithmetic mean observation-period excess return; CAGR is a geometric endpoint measure.

questions.question: What if volatility is zero?
questions.answer: The ratio is undefined. The calculator marks that condition instead of showing a real zero or infinity.

questions.question: Is multiplying by sqrt(12) always exact?
questions.answer: No. It is an annualization convention with assumptions about aggregation and serial correlation. It is not an exact compounded-return rule.

sources.title: William F. Sharpe: The Sharpe Ratio

black-scholes.summary: The Black-Scholes-Merton model values European call and put options using entered spot, strike, time, annual volatility and continuous interest and dividend rates. Theoretical value before expiry is different from a contract’s expiration payoff or a trader’s net profit.
black-scholes.scope: European exercise with constant annual volatility and continuous rates. Per-share theory values only; no American early exercise, discrete cash dividends, real-time quotes, implied-volatility estimation or employee-option accounting determination.

examples.title: Price a one-year European call with $100 spot and strike
examples.inputs: Spot $100; strike $100; one year to expiry; 20% annual volatility; 5% continuously compounded risk-free rate; zero continuous dividend yield.
steps: Use rates as decimals and time in years. The normal-distribution inputs are d1 = 0.35 and d2 = 0.15.
Evaluate S × N(d1) − K × exp(−rT) × N(d2) under the zero-dividend assumptions.
The result is a theoretical value per share. A contract multiplier, actual premium paid, fees and early exercise are separate questions.
examples.answer: The European call’s modeled value is about $10.450584 per share. It is neither an expiration profit nor a live option quote.

expected.label: European call theoretical value per share

questions.question: Are the results per share or per option contract?
questions.answer: Per share. The worksheet does not assume a contract multiplier or contract count, and its model price is not trading profit.

questions.question: Can I enter a negative risk-free rate?
questions.answer: Yes, within the displayed input range. It must be an annual continuously compounded rate consistent with the model.

questions.question: What happens at zero time or zero volatility?
questions.answer: Zero time gives intrinsic value. Zero volatility with time remaining uses the deterministic discounted spot/strike boundary.

questions.question: Does it value American early exercise?
questions.answer: No. It values European exercise under a constant continuous-dividend-yield assumption. American exercise and dated cash dividends require other treatment.
